reason: The provided sources contain 16 distinct claims corroborated across multiple independent websites regarding Uranus's discovery, orientation, weather, and space probe observations.
story: In 1781, astronomer William Herschel spotted a faint point of light through his homemade telescope and initially assumed it was a comet. It was actually Uranus, the first planet discovered in modern history. Uranus proved to be the coldest planet in the Solar System, with temperatures dropping to minus 224 degrees Celsius. It is also the only planet orbiting the Sun knocked completely on its side, with an axial tilt near 98 degrees likely caused by an ancient collision with a protoplanet. This extreme tilt subjects its poles to 42 years of continuous daylight followed by 42 years of total darkness during its 84-year orbit. Visited only once by NASA's Voyager 2 probe in 1986, Uranus surprised scientists with a wildly tilted magnetic field offset from its core. Decades later, scientists re-analyzing Voyager data discovered that Uranus had even flung a giant magnetic bubble of electrified hydrogen gas into space.
angle: Uranus orbits the Sun knocked completely on its side at nearly 98 degrees, causing each pole to endure 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of continuous darkness.

claims.claim: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781 using a telescope.
Herschel initially reported Uranus as a comet.
Herschel proposed naming the new planet Georgium Sidus in honor of King George III.
The planet was named Uranus after the Greek sky god following a suggestion by Johann Elert Bode.
Uranus takes approximately 84 Earth years to complete one orbit around the Sun.
Uranus completes one full rotation on its axis in about 17 hours.
Uranus has an extreme axial tilt of nearly 98 degrees, causing it to rotate sideways relative to its orbit.
Because of its extreme tilt, each pole receives about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of continuous darkness.
Scientists theorize that Uranus was knocked onto its side by a collision with a large protoplanet long ago.
Uranus is the coldest planet in the Solar System, with minimum atmospheric temperatures reaching minus 224 degrees Celsius.
Atmospheric methane absorbs red light, giving Uranus its characteristic blue-green or cyan appearance.
Wind speeds in Uranus's atmosphere reach up to 900 kilometers per hour (560 miles per hour).
Uranus's magnetic axis is offset from its center by one-third of the planet's radius and tilted roughly 60 degrees from its rotational axis.
NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft is the only probe ever to visit Uranus, flying past the planet in 1986.
Re-analyzed Voyager 2 data revealed that Uranus ejected a massive plasmoid bubble of electrified hydrogen gas into space.
Uranus's moons are named after literary characters created by William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

disputed: Moon count discrepancy: Source S1 lists 29 known moons, while source S2 lists 28 known moons; scripts should frame this as 28 or 29 known moons.

Protoplanet impact cause: Sources treat the collision that knocked Uranus on its side as a leading theory rather than absolute fact; scripts should attribute this as 'according to scientists' hypothesis'.

Magnetosphere compression state: Source S1 notes 2024 analysis suggesting Voyager 2 measured an anomalous compressed magnetosphere state due to rare space weather; scripts should attribute this finding to recent re-analysis.
